repo_cpu_config.evidence: wrangler.toml has no [limits], usage_model, placement, services, durable objects, queues or [env.*]; git grep finds no cpu_ms / usage_model / limits.cpu anywhere

deployed_version_metadata.read: wrangler versions view --json for e89ae509 (pre-resume disabled), a7760133 (resume-enabled), 0dee2b7a (post-resume disabled)
deployed_version_metadata.finding: identical script etag, handlers [fetch, scheduled], compatibility date and flags, assets, usage_model = standard on all three; no limits key; the readable metadata exposes no CPU limit value
deployed_version_metadata.deploy_lineage: every deploy used the same wrangler.toml and: npx wrangler deploy $(node scripts/deploy-identity.mjs --wrangler-vars) [--var DOSSIER_CANARY_ENABLED:true]; the only difference between enabled and disabled versions is that var
deployed_version_metadata.effective_plan_runtime_context: OWNER_CONFIRMED_PAID_BUT_NOT_MACHINE_VERIFIED (usage_model standard is consistent with Paid; the plan itself is not readable)

findings: Paid CPU per HTTP request: default 30 s, max 5 min; Free 10 ms
waiting on fetch, KV reads or database queries does NOT count as CPU time
limits are only supported for the Standard usage model and only enforced on the Cloudflare network; cpu_ms is set in Wrangler config or in the dashboard
each isolate has built-in flexibility for infrequent overruns of the configured limit; a Worker that hits the limit consistently is terminated according to the configured limit
exceeded CPU appears as Error 1102 to the client and outcome exceededCpu in analytics and Logpush
the Tail Handler page lists the outcome values (exceededCpu, exceededMemory) but does not define cpuTime or wallTime semantics for a terminated request: UNKNOWN officially

execution_topology.evidence: client -> public Worker fetch handler -> handleDossierCanary -> runner -> D1; no service binding, Durable Object, queue or second Worker exists in the configuration; the only fetch to another host happens in FETCH, not in DERIVE; the per-minute cron is a separate invocation of the same Worker (cpu 1-2 ms, ok)

tail_event_association.evidence: failed event POST /api/dossier/canary/run at 21:10:36.684Z on version a7760133; the run row lease was taken at 21:10:36.724Z (expires 21:12:36.724Z, 120 s) and the run progress was last updated 21:10:42.723Z, 6.0 s later, matching the event wall time of 6.6 s

cpu_telemetry_semantics.observation: successful invocations: 310-367 ms CPU over ~17.3 s wall for ~37 concepts (~8.5 ms CPU per concept). The failed invocation reported 119 ms after 6.6 s wall = ~14 concepts x ~8.5 ms, so the reported cpuTime is consistent with the work done before the kill (it looks like genuine accumulated CPU, not a partial or foreign counter).
cpu_telemetry_semantics.inference: a fixed per-invocation threshold below 367 ms is impossible (six invocations ran 310-367 ms on the same version); a 30 s limit cannot have been reached at 119 ms; so the enforcement that fired is not explained by any static limit, declared or default

candidate_explanations.D effective limit below 119 ms: contradicted by the successful invocations unless enforcement is statistical (isolate-level flexibility)

code_hotspot.evidence: per-concept DERIVE work is bounded by that concept's observations (live distribution: 384 concepts with 1, 10 with 2, one with 4, one with 6); no nested scan over all observations, aliases or concepts per concept; local profile (scripts/dossier-derive-cpu-profile.mjs): per-invocation Node CPU 46-109 ms for DERIVE slices of ~750 statements, per-concept CPU homogeneous (the 16 ms maxima are timer-tick artifacts)
code_hotspot.caveat: Node CPU is not Worker CPU

workload_shape.IS_D1_BUDGET_A_GOOD_CPU_PROXY: YES for this workload (CPU per invocation tracks statements: six slices within +-8%)
workload_shape.note: a good proxy for the amount of work, but it neither predicted nor prevented the kill

failure_position.attempt_1: died ~10 s wall into invocation 5 after ~20 concepts (derived 32 -> 52); no tail existed then
failure_position.resume_7: died 6.6 s wall into the invocation after ~14 concepts (derived ~274 -> 288)
failure_position.boundary_concepts: ordinary (1 observation each); the concept attempt 1 died on was processed successfully by the first resumed invocation
failure_position.FAILURE_PATTERN: SEMI_REPEATING (2 deaths in 9 DERIVE invocations, 0 in 3 INGEST; different positions and elapsed times; not tied to one concept)

CONFIGURED_CPU_LIMIT_TOO_LOW.evidence_against: no declared limit, no limits key in version metadata, six sibling invocations ran 310-367 ms
CONFIGURED_CPU_LIMIT_TOO_LOW.confidence: LOW that it is the cause

UNEXPECTED_EFFECTIVE_PLATFORM_LIMIT.evidence_for: kill at 119 ms of accurate-looking CPU; docs describe isolate-level flexibility and termination on consistent overrun
UNEXPECTED_EFFECTIVE_PLATFORM_LIMIT.evidence_against: no static limit fits the successes; effective plan limit not machine-verifiable

CHAINED_WORKER_CPU_LIMIT.confidence: HIGH that it is not the cause

APPLICATION_CPU_HOTSPOT.evidence_against: homogeneous bounded per-concept work; the same concept was later processed fine
APPLICATION_CPU_HOTSPOT.confidence: LOW that it is the cause

WORKLOAD_SLICE_TOO_LARGE.evidence_against: the killed invocation had used the least CPU of all (119 vs 310-367 ms)

CLOUDFLARE_PLATFORM_ANOMALY.evidence_for: random, non-position-bound deaths with healthy neighbours; documented isolate flexibility
CLOUDFLARE_PLATFORM_ANOMALY.evidence_against: two occurrences in a short window

decision.SAFE_MITIGATION_PATH: YES (limited): the risk is to run completion, never to GCOS safety; progress is durable per concept; a kill costs only a 120 s lease wait
decision.RESUME_2_TECHNICALLY_READY: NO until the one missing read-only fact is obtained: the Worker effective CPU limit and the CPU / invocation-status metrics (p99 CPU, exceeded-CPU series) from the Cloudflare dashboard or analytics
decision.MINIMUM_SAFE_FIX_CANDIDATE: (1) read the Worker CPU limit and the CPU and invocation-status metrics in the dashboard (read-only); (2) if the limit is not 30 s, correct it with limits.cpu_ms; (3) independently, reduce the per-invocation budget (e.g. 800 -> about 200 statements, ~85 ms expected CPU, since CPU tracks statements at ~0.42 ms each) and shorten the lease to ~45 s so a platform kill is recoverable within a minute; (4) keep the filtered tail capture. Step 3 is speculative with respect to the cause: the evidence does not prove that smaller slices avoid the kill.
